properties.name: Āliamanu Military Reservation

properties.name: Marine Corps Air Station ʻEwa
properties.note: Begun as a mooring mast for the Navy’s airships, never used by one; a Marine air station commissioned in 1941 (the State DOT’s history says 1942), the first hit in the attack of December 1941, closed in 1952 and taken into Barbers Point.

properties.name: Naval Air Station Barbers Point
properties.note: Kiawe and grazing land round the ʻEwa mooring mast, surveyed from 1940; field work began in 1941 and the station was commissioned in April 1942. Closed in 1999 (the State DOT’s history says 1998); the State’s Kalaeloa district was drawn round it.

properties.name: Waimānalo Military Reservation
properties.note: Set aside by executive order in 1917 on the Waimānalo shore; Bellows Field from 1933, its runway closed in 1958 and the Marines’ training ground from the 1950s. Parts went back to the State in 1966; today’s ground.

properties.name: Aiea Naval Hospital
properties.note: Cane land on the ridge above ʻAiea bought for a naval hospital, commissioned in 1942 and closed in 1949; the Marines’ Camp H. M. Smith from 1955, headquarters of the Pacific command.

properties.name: Center Combat Range
properties.note: Territorial land at Waipiʻo under a use permit for combat training from 1943; the Army gave notice that it had left in January 1946.

properties.name: Camp Kawaihapai
properties.note: A communications station on land beside the railway at Mokulēʻia from 1922 (the Corps of Engineers dates the first purchase to 1925); a fighter strip by the attack of 1941, enlarged in the war, an Air Force base named for Captain Dillingham in 1948 and the Army’s again from about 1975.

properties.name: Mokulēʻia Airfield runway
properties.note: Paved and lengthened in 1942–1945 until it could take the heavy bombers; Runway 08/26 as the FAA charts it.

properties.name: Fort Armstrong
properties.note: Built in 1907 on fill over the reef at Kakaʻako to guard Honolulu Harbor, headquarters of the coast artillery until 1922; given up by the Army about 1950 (FortWiki says 1949) and now part of the container port. Traced from the 1927 sheet.

properties.name: Fort DeRussy
properties.note: Bought at Kālia in 1904 for a coast artillery battery and named in 1909; the marsh behind the batteries was filled in the 1920s, and it has been a recreation centre for the armed forces since 1949.

properties.name: Fort Upton
properties.note: The coast artillery post on Queen Emma Point guarding the entrance to Pearl Harbor, taken by condemnation in 1907 and renamed Fort Kamehameha in 1909; its batteries were built 1907–1914 and its barracks from 1916. FortWiki ends it as a fortification in 1949; its ground passed to Hickam in 1992. The reservation as the 2000 sheet bounds it.

properties.name: Diamond Head Military Reservation
properties.note: Lēʻahi and its slopes, reserved by presidential order in 1906 for the harbour defences of Honolulu and named Fort Ruger in 1909; its mortar battery was built 1907–1910. Abandoned in 1955 (FortWiki).

properties.name: Fort Shafter
properties.note: The first permanent Army post on Oʻahu, built from 1905 on the Kahauiki Military Reservation, Crown land before annexation, and garrisoned and named in 1907; headquarters of the Army in the Pacific. Undeveloped land at its north end went to the State in 1983; today’s ground.

properties.name: Iroquois Point Military Reservation
properties.note: Reserved at Keʻahi Point on the west side of the Pearl Harbor entrance in 1899 (FortWiki); its gun battery was built 1921–1924 and it was named Fort Weaver in 1922, abandoned as a fort in 1948 and kept as a rifle range. The 1927 and 1938 sheets draw the reservation’s line where the range’s is today.

properties.name: Haleʻiwa Landing Field
properties.note: Leased at Puʻena Point from the Bishop Estate in 1917 for gunnery and emergency landings, enlarged in 1941, and the one field whose fighters rose against the attack of December 1941; closed in 1946, the lease ran out in 1948.

properties.name: Helemano Military Reservation
properties.note: A communications site, now housing; the 2000 sheet is the first read that bounds it.

properties.name: Hickam Field
properties.note: The airdrome on cane land and old reef between the harbour channel, John Rodgers Airport and Fort Kamehameha, taken by condemnation and dedicated in 1935 and activated in 1938. Part of the ground it held went to the Territory for the airport. Today’s ground of the joint base south of the Navy’s line.

properties.name: Kaʻena Point Military Reservation
properties.note: A fire control station and reservation acquired in 1923 and granted to the State in 1984, now a natural area reserve.

properties.name: Kaʻena Point Satellite Tracking Station
properties.note: Leased in part from the State; its lease is one of those signed in 1964, the first record read of it.

properties.name: Kahuku Training Area
properties.note: The Army’s training land in the hills behind Kahuku, owned in part and leased in part; its lease is one of those signed in 1964, the first record read of it. The wartime Kahuku Training Camp lay below it from 1943.

properties.name: Kuwaʻaohe Military Reservation
properties.note: Set aside on Mōkapu round Ulupaʻu in 1918; Camp Ulupaʻu in 1941 and Fort Hase in 1942, a coast artillery post until 1949, its ground then the Navy’s until the Marines came. Bounded where the 1927 sheet draws the reservation’s line.

properties.name: Naval Air Station Kāneʻohe Bay
properties.note: A seaplane base begun in 1939 and commissioned in 1941; in 1940 the Navy took the rest of Mōkapu, dredged the bay and filled the peninsula’s west shore. Decommissioned in 1949 and held by a small detail until the Marines took it.

properties.note: Ammunition storage in Kīpapa Gulch, mostly unused; the land-use plan of 2021 is the first record read that shows it.

properties.name: Lualualei naval reservation
alt: Naval Magazine Pearl Harbor, Lualualei Annex
properties.note: The Territory set land at Lualualei aside for the Navy in 1933; its radio transmitter site was activated in 1936, and the valley also holds the Navy’s magazines. Today’s ground; the record read does not date the magazine’s own taking.

properties.name: Makapuʻu Point Military Reservation
properties.note: Acquired by executive order in 1907 for a fire control station, and used for training through the war and until 1987.

properties.name: Mākua Military Reservation
properties.note: Mākua Valley, owned in part, ceded land in part and leased in part; its lease is one of those signed in 1964, the first record read of it. Live-fire training last took place in 2004.

properties.name: Pacific Jungle Combat Training Center
properties.note: Kahana and Punaluʻu valleys, held by lease, license and informal agreement for jungle warfare training from 1943; Kahana was given up in 1946 and the last Punaluʻu parcels in 1950.

properties.name: Pearl Harbor
properties.note: Puʻuloa. Under the convention proclaimed by Kalākaua in 1887 the United States had the exclusive right to enter the harbour and to keep a coaling and repair station there; it was the Navy’s harbour after annexation, its bar dredged from 1901. The lochs as the moku layer’s shore and a line across the entrance bound them; the convention gave a right over the water, not the land round it.

properties.name: Naval Station, Hawaiʻi
properties.note: The station was set up in Honolulu in 1899 and named for Hawaiʻi in 1900; condemnation of the yard’s ground at Pearl Harbor, Kuahua and a strip of Ford Island began in 1901, and the Act of 1908 made the navy yard, its drydock opened in 1919. Today’s naval ground of the joint base, which grew round the first taking; its line with Hickam is the one the 2000 sheet draws.

properties.name: Ford Island
properties.note: Mokuʻumeʻume. Bought in 1917 for the Army’s and the Navy’s aviation; the Army’s field was named Luke Field in 1919 and shared the island with the Navy’s air station until the Army moved to Hickam, complete by the end of 1940, and left it to the Navy.

properties.name: West Loch naval magazine
properties.note: The Navy’s ammunition wharves and magazines on West Loch, established in the 1930s (the land-use plan of 2021).

properties.name: Dillingham Airfield
properties.note: The State’s general aviation field on the Army’s ground at Mokulēʻia, under lease from 1962; renamed Kawaihapai in 2001.

properties.name: John Rodgers Airport
properties.note: Dedicated on March 21, 1927 on marsh and reef at Keʻehi; its land runways were laid on fill dredged from the seaplane runways of the lagoon in the war, and it took ground from Hickam after. The airport’s ground of today less the Reef Runway.

properties.name: Runway 8/26
properties.note: The longest of the airport’s paved runways in the record of 1946, joined in 1951 to Hickam’s section into one runway; the 1946 record is the first read that gives it.

properties.name: Reef Runway
properties.note: The runway on the reef, completed in October 1977 to take the jets’ take-offs out over the sea.

properties.name: Reef Runway
properties.note: Land made on the reef off Keʻehi for a runway out over the water; work began in 1973 and it was completed in October 1977.

properties.name: Runway 4L/22R
properties.note: The shorter of the pair; the 2000 sheet is the first read that draws it.

properties.name: Runway 4R/22L
properties.note: Rebuilt and lengthened in the 1970s so that its approach lay over the water; the 2000 sheet is the first read that draws it as it is.

properties.name: Kalaeloa Airport
properties.note: The airfield of the Barbers Point air station, turned over to the State when the station closed and kept for general aviation.

properties.name: Runway 04L/22R
properties.note: One of the air station’s runways, kept by the airport; the history of 1945 names a main runway and a cross runway, but the 2000 sheet is the first read that draws this one.

properties.name: Runway 04R/22L
properties.note: One of the air station’s runways, kept by the airport; the history of 1945 names a main runway and a cross runway, but the 2000 sheet is the first read that draws this one.

properties.name: Runway 11/29
properties.note: One of the air station’s runways, kept by the airport; the history of 1945 names a main runway and a cross runway, but the 2000 sheet is the first read that draws this one.

properties.name: Farrington Highway
properties.note: From Waialua along the Mokulēʻia shore toward Kaʻena; its oldest bridge in the inventory is of 1934.

properties.name: Farrington Highway
properties.note: Up the Waiʻanae coast from Kahe to Keawaʻula, beside the railway; its oldest bridges in the inventory, at Waiʻanae and Mākaha, are of 1937.

properties.name: Interstate H-1
properties.note: The freeway’s first new stretch, from its western end at Makakilo to the Kunia interchange, opened in September 1966 (one route list says 1967).

properties.name: Interstate H-1
properties.note: From the Kunia interchange to the Waiawa interchange with H-2, opened in March 1969.

properties.name: Lunalilo Freeway
properties.note: The freeway through Honolulu, begun as the Mauka Arterial whose first stretch opened in 1953; taken into H-1 and completed to Kāhala in July 1969.

properties.name: Interstate H-1
properties.note: Extended east from Waiawa past Pearl Harbor to the Hālawa interchange in 1971.

properties.name: Interstate H-1
properties.note: Carried on from Hālawa past the airport to the Kahauiki interchange a stretch at a time, and finished in May 1986.

properties.name: Interstate H-2
properties.note: Up the central plain from Waiawa to Wahiawā; the first stretch opened in October 1974 and the last, over Kīpapa Gulch, in February 1977.

properties.name: Interstate H-3
properties.note: The piece of H-3 east of Mōkapu Saddle Road to the Marine base gate, opened in 1977 on a temporary connection.

properties.name: Interstate H-3
properties.note: The windward stretch from Kamehameha Highway across Kāneʻohe, completed in 1987, ten years before the tunnels joined it to Hālawa.

properties.name: Interstate H-3
properties.note: From Hālawa up the valley and through the Koʻolau to Kāneʻohe, opened on December 12, 1997 after decades of dispute.

properties.name: Interstate H-3

properties.name: Tetsuo Harano Tunnels
properties.note: The twin tunnels under the Koʻolau crest between Hālawa and Haʻikū valleys; portals as the 2000 sheet draws them.

properties.name: Kahekili Highway
properties.note: The western bypass of Kāneʻohe, completed in March 1972.

properties.name: Kalanianaʻole Highway
properties.note: From Kailua to Waimānalo; its bridges at Waimānalo are of 1924, the oldest the inventory lists on it.

properties.name: Kalanianaʻole Highway
properties.note: Along the Maunalua shore from Hawaiʻi Kai to ʻĀina Haina; its oldest bridge in the inventory, at Wailupe, is of 1930.

properties.name: Kalanianaʻole Highway
properties.note: Round Makapuʻu Point and along the cliffs to Hanauma; its oldest bridges in the inventory are of 1931.

properties.name: Kamehameha Highway
properties.note: The highway from Honolulu up the central plain to Wahiawā and on round the north shore and the windward coast, opened in 1921; its stretch from Kīpapa to Wheeler Field was rebuilt on two levels, completed in 1950.

properties.name: Kamehameha Highway
properties.note: From Wahiawā down to Haleʻiwa, part of the highway of 1921.

properties.name: Kamehameha Highway
properties.note: From Kāneʻohe to the foot of the Pali, part of the highway of 1921.

properties.name: Kamehameha Highway
properties.note: Round the north shore and down the windward coast to Kahaluʻu, part of the highway of 1921; its windward bridges are of 1922–1926.

properties.name: Joseph P. Leong Highway
properties.note: The bypass inland of Haleʻiwa town, opened in September 1996.

properties.name: Likelike Highway
properties.note: Up Kalihi valley and through the Koʻolau to Kāneʻohe, completed with its tunnels in 1960; the tunnels were the county’s and went to the State in 1998.

properties.name: Likelike Highway

properties.name: Wilson Tunnels

properties.name: Nimitz Highway
properties.note: Along the harbour and past the airport to Pearl Harbor, built in the 1940s: for the bases and the airport in the war by one account, among the harbour works after it by the State’s harbors history.

properties.name: Nuʻuanu Pali Road

properties.note: Into Kailua across Kawainui stream; its bridges there date from 1940, the oldest the bridge inventory lists on it.

properties.name: Kalanianaʻole Highway
properties.note: The new four-lane road from the foot of the Pali toward Kailua, opened on September 3, 1951 ahead of the Pali Highway.

properties.name: Pali Highway
properties.note: The four-lane highway up Nuʻuanu and through the Koʻolau, built in pieces from 1952; its windward side and the town-bound tunnels opened on May 11, 1957, the Kailua-bound tunnels in 1959 (the report also gives 1960), and the downtown connection on August 1, 1961.

properties.name: Pali Tunnels
properties.note: The longer of the two pairs of tunnels under Nuʻuanu Pali, blasted in 1955–1956; portals as the 2000 sheet draws them.

properties.name: Oʻahu Railway and Land Company
properties.note: Benjamin Dillingham’s narrow-gauge common carrier, opened from Honolulu to ʻAiea on November 16, 1889, the king’s birthday, and closed at the end of 1947; the double track to ʻAiea lasted to about 1959. Traced from the 1938 sheet.

properties.name: Oʻahu Railway and Land Company
properties.note: Past Pearl City and Waipahu to the ʻEwa plantation mill, reached by 1892. Traced from the 1938 sheet.

properties.name: Oʻahu Railway and Land Company
properties.note: Across the ʻEwa plain and up the Waiʻanae coast to the mill there, by 1895. After the company closed the Navy ran its ammunition trains from West Loch to Lualualei on this line until 1970, and the stretch from ʻEwa to Kahe is kept by a railway society. Traced from the 1938 sheet.

properties.name: Oʻahu Railway and Land Company
properties.note: Round Kaʻena Point to Haleʻiwa, where Dillingham built his hotel, opened in June 1897. Traced from the 1938 sheet.

properties.name: Oʻahu Railway and Land Company
properties.note: Past Waimea Bay to the Kahuku mill, finished in December 1898, the main line’s full length. Traced from the 1938 sheet.
